displayQuote: Why don't you come up and see me sometime?

meta.title: Who really said "Why don't you come up and see me sometime?"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Mae West's real line in She Done Him Wrong (1933) is "Why don't you come up sometime and see me?" The famous word order came from ads and I'm No Angel.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Why don't you come up and see me sometime?'?
meta.ogDescription: Mae West's real 1933 line was "Why don't you come up sometime and see me?" We trace how the word order got rearranged — and why she adopted the rewrite.

answer.label: Mae West — but the words are in the wrong order
answer.sourceLine: The line is genuinely hers, but the famous sentence is a rearrangement. In She Done Him Wrong (Paramount, 1933) Lady Lou says “Why don’t you come up sometime and see me? I’m home every evening” — whose first sentence is the wording AFI lists at No. 26 of its 100 Movie Quotes ↗. West did later speak the popular phrase — without the opening “Why don’t you” — in I’m No Angel (1933).

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: West’s Broadway play Diamond Lil (New York, 9 April 1928)
Lady Lou (Mae West), to Cary Grant’s Captain Cummings

source.excerpt: LADY LOU: I always did like a man in a uniform. That one fits you grand. Why don’t you come up sometime and see me? I’m home every evening. — CAPTAIN CUMMINGS: Yeah, but, I’m busy every evening. — LADY LOU: Busy? Say, what are you trying to do, insult me?
trail: In She Done Him Wrong (Paramount, 1933) Lady Lou tells Captain Cummings, “Why don’t you come up sometime and see me? I’m home every evening.” That exact wording is what AFI lists as No. 26 of its 100 Movie Quotes ↗.

The rearranged version was in circulation within months. Word Histories ↗ reproduces a “Screen Bulletins” item in The Dallas Morning News of 12 May 1933 calling “Come up and see me sometime” a national byword after the film, plus an Evening Star (Washington, D.C.) cinema advertisement of 3 August 1933 built around those words.

West then spoke the popular phrase herself. In I’m No Angel (Paramount, 1933) Tira ends a phone call, “And don’t forget — come up and see me sometime”; American Masters ↗ notes the wording there matched the advertising.

By 1938 she was settling the argument in the rewrite’s favour: a Minneapolis Star interview of 1 April 1938 ↗ reports West saying the line is not “Come up some time ’n see me” but “Come up and see me some time.”
source.cutTag: She tries again a beat later: “Why don’t you come up sometime, hmm?”
source.excerptNote: Dialogue as transcribed by Word Histories ↗ and PBS’s American Masters ↗. Note where “sometime” sits — before “and see me,” not at the end.

sourceLink.text: Word Histories: the full dialogue and the 1933 print record

source.rightsHolder: Paramount Pictures (1933 films); Universal Pictures now handles distribution of She Done Him Wrong through its EMKA division
source.rightsNote: Both films that carry this line — She Done Him Wrong and I’m No Angel — were published by Paramount in 1933, so the dialogue is still under US copyright in 2026; short quotation for identification and commentary is another matter, but the screenplays are not public domain. The film was adapted from West’s 1928 play Diamond Lil, and the sources consulted here place this line in the film rather than the play.

author.name: Mae West
author.heading: Who she was
author.bio: Born in Brooklyn on 17 August 1893, Mary Jane “Mae” West went from child vaudevillian to Broadway’s most prosecuted playwright — her 1926 play Sex got her a ten-day sentence on morals charges, of which she served eight, and her 1928 hit Diamond Lil gave Hollywood the character that became Lady Lou. She arrived at Paramount in 1932 and, within a year, had handed the language two catchphrases she largely wrote herself. She then spent decades cheerfully performing the misquoted version of her own most famous line, which is a fairly complete summary of how she operated.

cite.sourceCitation: She Done Him Wrong, directed by Lowell Sherman (Hollywood, CA: Paramount Productions, 1933). misattribution.heading: Right woman, wrong word order
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake quote hung on a famous name — it is a famous name’s line with the words shuffled. Three things get muddled.

items.who: “Why don’t you come up and see me sometime?”
items.why: The film says “Why don’t you come up sometime and see me?” — that is the form AFI ranks at No. 26 ↗, and Wikipedia’s list of film misquotes ↗ pairs the two explicitly.

She really does say the phrase — but in the other 1933 Cary Grant picture, and without the opening clause. Word Histories ↗ transcribes Tira signing off a phone call: “And don’t forget — come up and see me sometime.” Wikiquote ↗ notes she used it in Sextette too.

Asked to settle the argument, she picked the popular form. Word Histories ↗ reproduces Robert E. Murphy’s “Mae West Comes to Town” in The Minneapolis Star of 1 April 1938, reporting that she said it is not “Come up some time ’n see me” but “Come up and see me some time.”

misattribution.truthLine: Mae West is the right person and 1933 is the right year — but the sentence she delivered in She Done Him Wrong is “Why don’t you come up sometime and see me?”, and the version everyone repeats reached the public through advertising and her follow-up film, as American Masters ↗ lays out.

context.heading: Why the wrong version won
lead: Mae West’s original has a stumble in it. “Why don’t you come up sometime and see me?” buries the invitation in the middle of the sentence; the rearranged version saves the word “sometime” for the end, where it can be drawled. Wikipedia’s list of film misquotes ↗ makes exactly that point: the misquotation improves the rhythm.

The public was not alone in preferring it. Cinema advertising used the smoother wording — a 3 August 1933 Evening Star ad for the Metropolitan’s return engagement ran the words in quotation marks above West’s name — and PBS’s American Masters ↗ notes the phrase was used in ads for both pictures. By the time I’m No Angel opened later that year, West was saying the ad-copy version on screen, and she adopted the misquoted line for the rest of her life — she even recorded a song of the same name.
context.detailsSummary: What the actual scene sounds like
detailsBody: The exchange is a seduction played against a temperance officer. Lady Lou admires Captain Cummings’s uniform, issues the invitation, and gets a flat refusal — “I’m busy every evening” — which she treats as a challenge rather than an answer.

She tries again, shorter: “Why don’t you come up sometime, hmm?” Then the closer that also became a catchphrase in 1933: “you can be had.” The Dallas Morning News of 12 May 1933 listed both as new national bywords, which is a fair measure of how fast the film’s slang travelled.
context.pull: The public rewrote the line, the studio printed the rewrite, and then West started saying it that way herself.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Mae West page lists "Why don't you come up sometime and see me? … Come on up, I'll tell your fortune." under She Done Him Wrong (1933), notes it is widely said to be misquoted as "Why don't you come up and see me sometime?", and states West did say "come up and see me sometime" in I'm No Angel and Sextette.

Word Histories transcribes the full She Done Him Wrong exchange ("Why don't you come up sometime and see me? I'm home every evening." / "Yeah but, I'm busy every evening."), the I'm No Angel line "And don't forget – come up and see me sometime", the Dallas Morning News "Screen Bulletins" of 12 May 1933 calling the phrase a national byword, the Evening Star advertisement of 3 August 1933, and the Minneapolis Star of 1 April 1938 reporting West's own preferred wording "Come up and see me some time."

PBS American Masters states the signature line was first spoken as Lady Lou in the 1933 film She Done Him Wrong, that it began as "Why don't you come up some time and see me", that "Come up and see me sometime" was used in ads for both She Done Him Wrong and I'm No Angel and took on its now-popular wording in the latter, that West adopted the misquoted version for the rest of her life and recorded a song of the same name, and gives her dates as Aug 17, 1893 – Nov 22, 1980.
AFI's 100 Years…100 Movie Quotes lists at No. 26: "Why don't you come up sometime and see me?" — She Done Him Wrong (1933), production company Paramount Productions, Inc.

Wikipedia's List of film misquotes pairs the misquote "Why don't you come up and see me sometime?" with the actual line "Why don't you come up sometime and see me?" spoken by Lady Lou (Mae West) in She Done Him Wrong (1933), and notes the misquoted version improves the rhythm.

The AFI Catalog record for She Done Him Wrong gives release date 27 January 1933, production company and distributor Paramount Productions, Inc., and states it is based on the play Diamond Lil by Mae West (premiered New York, 9 April 1928).

Wikipedia's She Done Him Wrong article gives release 27 January 1933, Paramount Pictures, directed by Lowell Sherman, screenplay by Harvey F. Thew and John Bright from West's 1928 play Diamond Lil, with West as Lady Lou and Cary Grant as Captain Cummings; it notes the 1996 National Film Registry selection and that Universal Pictures handles distribution through its EMKA division.
Wikipedia's Mae West article gives her birth as August 17, 1893 in Brooklyn and death November 22, 1980 in Los Angeles, and covers her plays Sex (1926) and Diamond Lil (1928).
Quote Investigator's Mae West tag page has no article on "come up and see me sometime" — the nine listed articles cover other Mae West quotes, so QI has not adjudicated this line.
